meta.blurb: Leila's pay vanishes every month, and she cannot say where it goes. Over ginger tea, a retired shopkeeper gives her one question that sorts everything she owns or owes into two groups. Even a car needs a closer look.
meta.bible: Leila: a young woman of about twenty-two with her first full-time job at a garden centre; curious, honest and a little embarrassed about money. Mr Okafor: her neighbour, about seventy, a retired shopkeeper who ran a small hardware shop for forty years; patient, dry-humoured and kind; he drinks ginger tea and keeps a thick notebook. Money is counted in dollars. Leila's pay is two thousand dollars a month after tax. About four hundred dollars a month went on small things she hardly noticed. Her starting net worth is about minus two thousand dollars: a little over one thousand dollars of savings, laptop and bicycle, against a student loan and phone payments of more than three thousand. A year later her net worth has risen by almost four thousand dollars. Key terms: Asset, Liability, Income, Expenses, Inflation, Interest, Compound, Mortgage, Debt, Diversification, Bond, Bonds, Fund, Share, Shares, Net worth, Emergency fund, Insurance, Tax, Bookkeeping, Carpentry, Programming, Landlady, Tenant, Garden centre. Mr Okafor's shop story: a bright new sign did little, a second fridge for cold drinks paid for itself within a season. The one question: does this put money in my pocket, or take it out? The book teaches general principles only, does not name any real brand or person, and is not personal financial advice; tax rules differ by country. Voice: warm, plain, practical and never preachy; every fact is true and hedged where it depends on the country or the market. Fixed figures: Leila's savings about six hundred dollars, laptop about four hundred, bicycle about one hundred and fifty; student loan about two thousand seven hundred dollars at about four percent a year; phone payment plan about five hundred dollars left at about twelve percent a year. Her net worth at the start is therefore about minus two thousand dollars. She plans to save two hundred and fifty dollars every payday month and pay off her phone first. People: Mrs Varga, Leila's landlady, about sixty, brisk and fair, rents Leila a room in an old house; Dani, Leila's friend and workmate, bought a second-hand car and a credit card; Mr Banda, a taxi driver who earns his living with his car; Mr Haddad, the baker, bakes bread before dawn and bought a bigger oven on a loan; Ms Rowan, the manager of the garden centre; Mrs Lind, the evening tutor of Leila's bookkeeping class; Tomas, Leila's younger brother, about fifteen. Mr Okafor's shop was called Okafor Hardware. In the autumn Mr Okafor visits his daughter for a month and Leila keeps to her plan alone. At the end Leila's net worth is positive for the first time. Examples use made-up amounts, and nothing in the book is personal financial advice. Leila holds a certificate in garden management from her college years. Her extra bookkeeping work for Ms Rowan earns about one hundred dollars a month, which she sends to her phone plan.

B1B2: Leila has just received her first full pay from the garden centre, and the number on the slip looks wonderful. Two thousand dollars after tax is more money than she has ever had at once.

Every morning Leila carries heavy trays of young plants onto the shop floor and answers questions from customers. She does not know every plant yet, but she is learning quickly and she enjoys the work.
To celebrate her pay, Leila buys a new jacket and takes two friends out for a big dinner. For one whole evening she feels like the richest person in the city.
By the middle of the month, Leila notices that the balance on her phone is much smaller than she expected. She tells herself that rent and bills are due, so it must be normal.
When the month ends, almost nothing is left of her pay, and Leila cannot say where it has gone. She has not bought anything large, and that is what bothers her most.
Her neighbour Mr Okafor, who is about seventy, comes down the stairs with a small watering can. He sees her frowning at her phone and stops to ask what is wrong.
Mr Okafor says that most problems look smaller over a cup of tea. He leads her into his kitchen, which smells of fresh ginger and old wood.
On the kitchen wall hang old photographs of a small hardware shop with a painted sign. Mr Okafor tells her that he ran it for forty years before he retired.
Leila looks down at her cup and admits that she feels foolish. She works hard every day, yet at the end of the month she has nothing to show for it.
Mr Okafor smiles and says that she is far from foolish, because nobody ever teaches money in plain words. He tells her that it is really not complicated.
Mr Okafor writes one question on the paper in large pencil letters. It says, does this put money in my pocket, or take money out?
Mr Okafor says that anything which puts money in your pocket, or grows in value, is called an asset. He compares it to a tomato plant that gives fruit every summer.
A liability, he says, is the opposite: it takes money out of your pocket. He draws a leaking bucket, with coins dripping slowly from a hole in the bottom.
Next, he draws a line down the middle of the paper and writes asset on one side and liability on the other. He promises that the question will sort almost anything she owns.
First, Leila tries the question on her laptop, which she bought for study. It helps her learn new things, and she decides that it might help her earn money one day.
Next comes her bicycle, which is harder to decide. It saves her the bus fare every day, but its tyres wear out and she pays for repairs.
Then she thinks about her phone, which she needs for work and for talking to her family. Every month, however, she still has to pay for it, and the payments take money out of her pocket.
Mr Okafor tells her that the columns are not a test, and nobody is being judged. They are only a way of seeing clearly, and a clear view is the first thing a person needs.
He tells her that most people never write down what they own and what they owe. They carry the numbers around in their heads, where they are blurry, and a blurry number is easy to ignore.
Before she leaves, he gives her a spare notebook with a pencil tucked into the spine. Her homework is to list everything she owns, everything she owes, and every payment she makes for a month.
That evening Leila sits at her small kitchen table and opens a full month of bank records. She has never looked at them line by line before.
She draws two columns in her notebook and heads them income and expenses. Income is the money that comes in each month, and expenses are everything that goes out again.
First she circles the large payments she expects every month, such as rent, electricity and the loan. These are fixed costs, and she is not surprised by any of them.
Next she finds the small purchases, a coffee here and a sandwich there. Alone, none of them is large, but the list is very long, and the lines keep coming.
Then she finds three monthly subscriptions that she had almost forgotten. One was a film service that she had not used for two months, and she feels her cheeks grow warm.
Late at night, after a tiring shift, she had taken a few taxis and ordered a few meals to be delivered. Each one felt like a small reward, but the fees at the bottom were larger than the food.
Leila adds up all these small payments with a calculator, and the total is about four hundred dollars. It is not rent or a bill, and it is not anything she chose on purpose.
Four hundred dollars is a fifth of her whole pay, and she stares at the number for a long time. It means that for every five dollars she earns, one dollar slips out through the leaks.
On Sunday she shows Mr Okafor her list, expecting him to scold her. Instead he reads it carefully and says that every shop in the world has leaks.
Mr Okafor tells her that when he first counted his stock, he found small, steady losses everywhere. Some goods were damaged, some were never recorded, and together they were costing him a great deal.
In the evening, Leila checks the money she has saved so far. It is about six hundred dollars, and she has kept it in the bank for almost two years.
Mr Okafor says that cash in the bank is an asset, because she can use it whenever she needs it. Its main job is to be safe and ready for emergencies.
Mr Okafor takes an old price tag out of a drawer. When he opened his shop, a plastic bucket cost about a quarter of what it costs today.
This slow rise in prices is called inflation, and it happens in most countries most of the time. The speed changes from year to year, but it rarely stops completely.
When prices rise, the same amount of money buys a little less than before. If your cash stays in a drawer, it holds its number but slowly loses its strength.
Her bank pays her a small amount of interest for keeping her money there. Sometimes the interest is higher than inflation, but sometimes it is lower, and nobody can promise which.
Mr Okafor puts two bags on the table, one marked needs and one marked investments. Money that she will need soon, he says, belongs in cash, where its value will not suddenly fall.
Money she will not need for many years, however, might be able to do more than sit still. A seed that stays in the packet never becomes a plant.
Leila asks if she should take all her savings out of the bank right away. Mr Okafor shakes his head and says that she needs to learn before she acts.
Back in her room, Leila writes a full list of everything she owns, with a rough value beside each item. Her savings, her laptop and her bicycle are the only things that are worth much.
At work, Leila's friend Dani proudly shows her a second-hand car that she has just bought. It is small, blue and very shiny, and Dani cannot stop smiling.
Leila asks gently about the running costs, and Dani counts them on her fingers. Fuel, insurance and parking come to a good deal more than she had expected.
Then there are the repairs, which never arrive on a convenient day. A second-hand car may run for months without trouble, and then need a large repair in a single morning.
Mr Okafor, who has joined them at the car park, adds that most cars also lose value every year. People call this depreciation, and it begins as soon as the car leaves the shop.
Dani takes out her phone and adds up every cost in a list. The total shows how many hours of her work each month go into keeping the car on the road.
Mr Okafor then points to Mr Banda, a taxi driver, who is waiting for a customer on the corner. His car earns money every day, and every cost of it is part of a working business.
So the same object can be an asset for one person and a liability for another. What matters is not the thing itself, but what it does for your money.
Leila looks again at her own bicycle, which she had been unsure about. It saves her the bus fare every working day, so she decides that it is a small asset, even though it needs repairs.
Mr Okafor says that his rule is not that cars are bad, and that many people need one for work or for family. The rule is simply to ask what the car does, and to count its cost honestly.
Dani decides to keep the car, because she needs it for her long journey to work. She offers a colleague a lift and asks for help with the fuel, to cut her costs.
Leila lives in a small room on the top floor of an old house. The house belongs to her landlady, Mrs Varga, who is brisk, fair and very fond of the garden.
On the first day of each month, Leila gives Mrs Varga an envelope with the rent. It is an expense, because the money goes out every month and she never owns the room.
Mr Okafor owns his small house, with the green door and the ginger plants on the windowsill. He finished paying for it nearly ten years ago, after a very long loan.
Most people cannot pay for a whole house at once, so they borrow the money from a bank. This kind of loan is called a mortgage, and it is paid back with interest over many years.
Owning a home does not stop the costs, because roofs leak and pipes break. There are also taxes, insurance and bills, and they arrive whether the owner is ready or not.
Over many years, the price of a home has often risen, but it has not done so everywhere or at every time. Sometimes prices have stood still for years, and sometimes they have fallen.
Mr Okafor says that your own home can be both an asset and a liability at once. It is an asset if its value rises, and a liability when its monthly costs take your money out.
Mrs Varga owns the old house, and she rents several rooms to people like Leila. For her, the monthly rent is money coming in, so the house may be an asset.
Mr Okafor says, however, that rent is not pure profit. There are empty months when no one pays, and there are repairs, taxes and a loan that the owner must still pay.
Leila nervously asks Mrs Varga about her costs, and Mrs Varga laughs and fetches her own list. It is long, and Leila sees that the owner's side of the rent is not simple either.
Mr Okafor explains that debt is simply money that you borrow and must pay back. Usually the lender also asks for a little extra, called interest.
Interest is the price of borrowing, a little like the rent on money. The higher the rate, the more it costs to use someone else's cash for a year.
Leila turns to her own debts, starting with the student loan. She still owes about two thousand seven hundred dollars, and the interest rate is about four percent a year.
Mr Okafor says that some debts can help a person earn more, and a loan for study may be one. If the training leads to a better job, then the loan has worked for the borrower.
Her phone plan is a different kind of debt. About five hundred dollars are still to be paid, and the plan charges roughly twelve percent interest a year.

Dani shows Leila her credit card bill, and a very high percentage is printed in small letters at the bottom. Credit cards often charge much more than a bank loan, sometimes twenty percent a year or higher.
If you pay only the minimum amount each month, most of the money goes to interest. The debt can last for years and cost far more than the thing you originally bought.
Mr Okafor tells her that in his shop he once allowed some customers to pay later. Some did pay, but others forgot, and he learned that giving credit costs the lender too.
Borrowing to buy something that earns money, like a good tool, can make sense. Borrowing to buy something that only gives pleasure usually costs more than it gives back.
Mr Okafor says that debt is a sharp tool, and a sharp tool can build a house or cut a hand. Before signing anything, she should check the rate, the length of the loan and the total cost.
Mr Okafor draws a long hill and puts a small snowball at the top. He says that this is the best picture he knows for how interest behaves.
When a debt is not paid, the interest is added to the amount owed. Next month the interest is charged on the bigger amount, and the snowball begins to grow.
Suppose someone owes one thousand dollars at twenty percent and pays nothing. After one year the debt is about twelve hundred dollars, and after five years it is about twenty-five hundred.
Leila stares at the numbers and suddenly understands why Dani's credit card balance never seems to fall. The interest is arriving faster than Dani's small payments can remove it.
Then Mr Okafor turns the paper around and shows that the same snowball can roll in the other direction. The same force that works against a borrower can work for a saver.
Suppose someone saves one thousand dollars at five percent a year and leaves it alone. After ten years it has grown to about sixteen hundred and thirty dollars, and the saver has only had to wait.
Mr Okafor tells her that time is the most important part of the snowball. Someone who starts early with a small amount often finishes ahead of someone who starts late with a larger amount.
There is a rough rule that people use, called the rule of seventy-two. Divide seventy-two by the yearly rate, and you get the approximate number of years that money takes to double.
Mr Okafor warns that real investments do not grow in a smooth line like the examples on paper. Some years they rise, some years they fall, and no rate is ever a promise.
Leila looks at her own papers and realises that she is riding two snowballs at the same time. One is a small saving that grows, and the other is a loan that charges her interest.
Next Mr Okafor explains what a share is, using a shop as an example. When a company sells shares, each share is a small piece of ownership, and the buyer becomes a part-owner.
If the company earns well, people want its shares and the price may rise. If the company does badly, the price can fall, and an owner can lose some of the money she paid.
Some companies also pay out a part of their profit to the owners of their shares. This payment is called a dividend, and it is another way that shares can put money in your pocket.
Share prices can jump around a great deal from week to week. People who panic and sell during a fall often lose money, because they sell at the lowest point.
Mr Okafor remembers a customer who bought a share and sold it a month later in fear. The price rose again the next year, and the man never forgave himself.
Mr Okafor says that buying one share is like betting on one horse. A fund puts the money of many people into a large basket of shares, which spreads the risk.
This idea of spreading money across many things has a long name, diversification. Mr Okafor prefers the old saying about not putting all your eggs in one basket.
Funds charge a fee for their work, and this cost comes out of the money in the fund. A small difference in fees can add up to a large difference after many years.
Mr Okafor says that money she will need soon should never be put in shares. Prices can fall just when you need to sell, and then you are forced to accept a loss.
Leila says she does not feel ready to buy anything yet. Mr Okafor agrees, and reminds her that everything he says is general, not advice for her own life.
Mr Okafor moves on to a different kind of asset, called a bond. A bond is a loan that you make to a company or a government, and in return you receive interest.
The borrower promises to pay interest at regular times and to return the original money at the end of a set period. That date is fixed in advance, which many people find comforting.
Bonds are usually steadier than shares, but they are not free of risk. A company can fail to pay, and even a government can have trouble, though that is rarer.
A savings account is the simplest asset that Leila has, and the one she knows best. It pays a little interest, and the bank holds her money until she asks for it.
Many countries protect bank deposits up to a certain amount, but the rules differ from place to place. Mr Okafor urges her to find out exactly what protection applies where she lives.
Mr Okafor then shows her a simple idea about risk and reward. Safe things tend to grow slowly, while riskier things may grow faster, and they may also fall.
Mr Okafor puts three glass jars on a shelf and labels them safe, steady and growing. He says that a person can use all three for different jobs.
Leila draws her own three jars in her notebook and writes a small number next to each. Almost everything is in the safe jar, and the other two are nearly empty.
By now Leila has learned that assets come in many kinds, from cash to shares to a business. Each one has its own risk, its own reward and its own time to grow.
Leila puts down her pencil and realises that none of it is magic. It is only a set of careful choices, made over many months, by someone who keeps looking at the numbers.
One early morning, before her shift, Leila walks past a small bakery where the lights are already on. The smell of warm bread fills the whole street, and she stops to look through the window.
The baker, Mr Haddad, laughs and says that a bakery has many costs besides flour. He pays rent, wages, gas and electricity, and the bread must pay for every one of them.
Mr Okafor, who sometimes buys his bread there, says that a business is an asset only when it earns more than it costs. The oven and the shop are tools, but the profit is the proof.
Mr Haddad tells her that two years ago he borrowed money to buy a bigger oven. It lets him bake twice as much bread in the morning, and the extra sales have paid for it.
Mr Haddad adds that not every week is good. When it rains for days, fewer people come into the shop, and the bread that he cannot sell must be thrown away.
Mr Okafor tells Leila about a mistake from his own shop. He once spent a large amount on a bright new sign, and he was sure that it would bring in crowds of customers.
Soon afterwards he bought a second fridge for cold drinks, because many customers had asked for them in summer. It cost much less than the sign, and it paid for itself within one season.
Mr Okafor explains that he had not guessed about the fridge. He had counted for a month how often customers asked for cold drinks, and the tally marks made the decision for him.
The lesson, Mr Okafor says, is to test small before spending big. Whether it is a fridge or an investment, a small trial costs little and teaches a lot.
The next morning, Leila looks at the garden centre with new eyes. She sees the plants as stock, the greenhouse as a tool, and the till as the place where the proof appears.
Inspired by the bakery, Leila signs up for an evening class in bookkeeping. It meets twice a week in a plain classroom above a library, and the fee is a few hundred dollars.
Her tutor, Mrs Lind, is strict, tidy and very funny when she forgets to be strict. She teaches the class to write down every sale and every cost in the right column.
Mr Okafor says that a skill can be an asset, because it can raise the money a person earns. It cannot be sold or stolen, and it often grows more valuable with use.
Mr Okafor reminds her that a course has a cost, and the benefit is never guaranteed. She should weigh what it costs in money and time against what it might bring.
In class she practises with a pretend shop, writing each sale and cost in two neat columns. Every week she finds her mistakes, and every week there are fewer of them.

Over long periods, the price of a home has often risen, which is one reason people see houses as assets, but it has not done so in every place or in every decade. Sometimes prices have stood still for years, and sometimes they have fallen quite sharply, leaving owners owing more than the house was worth. Mr Okafor said that nobody should buy a home on the promise that it will certainly get richer.

Your own home, Mr Okafor concluded, can be both an asset and a liability at the same time, and the honest answer depends on the numbers. It may grow in value over the years, which helps, but every month it takes money out for the loan, the repairs and the bills. A wise buyer, he said, looks carefully at both of the arrows on the page before signing anything at all.

Mrs Varga, on the other hand, owned the old house, and she rented rooms to people like Leila, which meant that every month money came in. For her, the very same envelope that Leila counted as an expense was income, and so the house could be placed in the asset column. Leila found it strange, and a little dizzying, to realise that her own rent was somebody else's earnings.

Mr Okafor was quick to add that rent is not pure profit, as many people imagine it to be. There are empty months when no tenant pays, there are repairs, taxes and insurance, and often there is also a loan that the owner must go on paying. A rental home only deserves a place in the asset column, he said, when the income really does beat the costs.

Leila nervously asked Mrs Varga about her costs, expecting to be told that it was none of her business, but the landlady only laughed and fetched a long list from the kitchen drawer. It included the roof, the heating, the taxes, the insurance and a plumber's invoice that made Leila wince. She left the kitchen with a new respect for the other side of the rent envelope.

Debt, Mr Okafor said, is simply money that you borrow and promise to pay back at some later date. Usually the lender also asks for something extra in return for waiting, and that extra amount is called interest. It was such a plain description that Leila wondered why it had always sounded so frightening.

Interest, he went on, is the price of borrowing, a little like the rent that Leila paid for her room, except that here it was the money that was rented. The higher the rate, the more it costs to use somebody else's cash for a year, so the rate is always the first thing to read. Most people, he said, read the size of the monthly payment and completely ignore the rate that sits behind it.

Leila turned to her own debts, beginning with the student loan from her college years. She still owed about two thousand seven hundred dollars, and the interest rate was about four percent a year, which Mr Okafor called gentle. The rate on that loan, he said, is the main reason it can be handled calmly.

Not every debt is an enemy, Mr Okafor said, because some of them help a person to earn more than they could have earned without them. A loan for study is a good example, since a certificate may lead to a better job, and a better job can repay the loan many times over. Leila thought of her certificate in garden management, and of how it had won her the job at the garden centre.

Her phone plan was a different kind of debt, and a more expensive one. About five hundred dollars were still to be paid, and the plan charged roughly twelve percent interest a year, three times the rate of the student loan. She had signed the contract in a shop, in a hurry, without reading the line that mattered most.

Dani brought her credit card statement to the garden centre canteen, and she pointed at a very high percentage printed in small letters at the bottom. Credit cards often charge far more interest than a bank loan, sometimes twenty percent a year or even more, depending on the country and the card. Dani groaned aloud, because until that moment she had believed that the only cost was the monthly payment.

Mr Okafor warned that if a person pays only the minimum amount each month, most of the payment goes straight to interest, and the original debt hardly shrinks. The balance can then last for years and end up costing far more than the thing that was bought in the first place. “It is a road,” he said, “that is very easy to enter and very slow to leave.”

Mr Okafor told her that early in his career he had allowed some trusted customers to buy now and pay later, and he had written their names in a ledger. Some of them paid on time, some paid late and a few never paid at all, and he learned that credit has a cost for the person who gives it, too. After that painful lesson he charged a small fee for waiting and kept his customers' accounts much shorter.

Mr Okafor drew two doors on the paper, one for borrowing to buy something that earns money and one for borrowing to buy something that only gives pleasure. The first door can make sense, as when a baker borrows for an oven, while the second usually costs more than it gives back. Leila noticed, with a small wince, that her own phone had gone through the second door without any hesitation.

Debt is a sharp tool, Mr Okafor said, and a sharp tool can build a house or cut a hand, depending entirely on who is holding it. Before signing any paper, Leila should always check the interest rate, the length of the loan and the total amount that she will have paid at the end. He wrote those three things in the margin of her notebook and underlined them twice.

Mr Okafor drew a long hill on a clean page and put a small snowball at the very top of it. He tapped the little circle with his pencil and said that this was the best picture he knew for how interest behaves, in both good ways and bad. Leila leaned closer, because she had a feeling that this lesson mattered more than the others.

When a debt is left unpaid, he explained, the interest is added to the amount owed, and the next month's interest is calculated on the larger total. That means the debt now earns interest on its own interest, and the snowball picks up speed with every turn. The bigger it grows, the faster it grows, which is why small debts can become frightening ones.

He gave her an example with simple numbers: suppose someone owes one thousand dollars at twenty percent a year and pays nothing at all. After one year the debt is about twelve hundred dollars, and after five years it has grown to about twenty-five hundred. The person has borrowed one thousand and now owes two and a half times as much.

Leila stared at the numbers, and she suddenly understood why Dani's credit card balance never seemed to shrink, however faithfully Dani paid. The interest was arriving almost as fast as her small payments could remove it, like a bath filling while someone is trying to empty it with a cup. She decided, there and then, to say something kind and useful to Dani at lunch the next day.

Then Mr Okafor turned the paper around, and the hill seemed to change its direction, so that the same snowball was now rolling in the saver's favour. The very force that grows a borrower's debt can also grow a saver's pile, because the earnings are added to the money and begin to earn earnings of their own. It was the same machine pointing the opposite way, and Leila felt a small shock of delight.

He gave her a second example: if someone saves one thousand dollars at five percent a year and leaves it alone for ten years, it grows to about sixteen hundred and thirty dollars. The saver has done nothing in all that time except wait, and the extra six hundred and thirty dollars was earned by the money itself. He added that the same pile would be about twenty-six hundred and fifty dollars after twenty years.

Time, Mr Okafor told her, is the most important ingredient in the whole recipe, and it is the only one that cannot be bought. Someone who starts early with a small amount can finish ahead of someone who starts much later with a larger amount, simply because the snowball has had more hill to roll down. Leila wished, with a pang, that somebody had told her all of this when she was sixteen years old.

There is a rough rule of thumb that people use, he said, called the rule of seventy-two, and it is easy to remember. If you divide seventy-two by the yearly rate of growth, you get the approximate number of years that money takes to double, so at seven percent it is about ten years. It is only an estimate, he reminded her, and real life is a good deal bumpier than a tidy sum on paper.

Mr Okafor warned that real investments never grow in the smooth, tidy lines of examples on paper, and that no rate of return is ever a promise. Some years they rise strongly, some years they fall, and long-term averages hide a great many uncomfortable months in between. He drew a wavy line on the page next to the straight one, so that she would remember the difference.

Leila looked at her own papers, laid out side by side on Mr Okafor's table, and she realised that she was riding two snowballs at the same time. One was a modest savings account that earned a little, and the other was a pair of debts that charged her rather more, so the larger of the two was pulling in the wrong direction. The question that remained was which of the two she would choose to feed from now on.

Next, Mr Okafor explained what a share is, and he used the shop on the corner as an example. If the owner divided the business into a thousand equal pieces and sold some of them, each piece would be a share, and each buyer would become a very small part-owner. It was a surprisingly simple idea for something that appeared on the news every evening.

If the company earns well, he said, more people want its shares and the price may rise, and if the company does badly the price can fall just as easily. An owner of shares therefore takes a part in both the good news and the bad, and may lose some of the money she put in. That uncertainty is why shares are called risky, although a great many people hold them for decades.

Some companies also share part of their profit with their owners, in a payment called a dividend, which arrives every few months or once a year. It is another way in which a share can put money in the owner's pocket, in addition to any rise in its price. Mr Okafor cautioned that not all companies pay one, and none can promise to keep paying.

Share prices can jump about in a most alarming way from week to week, and sometimes from hour to hour. People who panic and sell during a fall often lose money that they might have recovered if they had waited, because they sell at exactly the lowest point. Mr Okafor said that most of the damage in investing comes from fear, rather than from the market itself.

Mr Okafor remembered a customer from his shop who had bought a few shares with his savings and then watched the price fall in the first month. In a panic, the man sold them at a loss, and a year later the price had risen above what he first paid. He told the story without a trace of cruelty, only with a kind of weary understanding for the poor man's fear.

Buying a single company's shares, Mr Okafor said, is like betting on one horse in a very long race. A fund gathers the money of many people and spreads it over a large basket of different shares, so that one company's failure hurts less. It does not remove the risk, but it makes the risk easier to carry.

This habit of spreading money across many different things has a long name, diversification, which Mr Okafor said he had never learned to say without stumbling. He preferred the old saying about not putting all your eggs in one basket, and he demonstrated it with six eggs and three small baskets from his kitchen. Leila laughed out loud, and promised him solemnly that she would not drop any of the eggs on the way home.

Funds charge a fee for managing the money, he added, and this cost is quietly taken out of what the owner would otherwise have earned. A small difference in fees can add up to a surprisingly large difference after thirty years, so it is worth reading the small print. He tapped her notebook and told her to add fees to the list of things she should always check.

Money that she would need within a few years, Mr Okafor said, should never be placed in shares, because prices may fall just at the moment when she needs to sell. Shares suit money that can wait for a long time and ride out the bumps, while cash suits money that must be ready next month. The difference between the two, he said, is simply a matter of the calendar and of how soon the money is needed.

Leila admitted that she did not yet feel ready to buy anything, and Mr Okafor said that she was quite right to feel that way. Learning comes before buying, he said, and everything he told her was only general knowledge, never advice fitted to her own life or her own country. Anyone facing a truly large decision, he added gravely, should read the small print slowly and consult a qualified professional.

Mr Okafor moved on to bonds, and he began by reminding her that she knew something about loans already. A bond is a loan that you make to a company or a government, and in return you receive interest, so you are the bank rather than the borrower. Leila liked the idea of sitting on the other side of the table for once.

The borrower promises to pay interest at regular times and to return the original money on a date fixed in advance, which might be five or ten years away. That fixed date and the regular payments make a bond feel more predictable than a share, and many people find it comforting. Mr Okafor compared it to lending a neighbour a ladder with an agreed day for its return.

Bonds are usually steadier than shares, he said, but he refused to call them safe, because no investment deserves that word without a condition. A company may fail to pay its debts, and a government may have trouble too, though the chance depends heavily on who is borrowing and on the country. A careful lender, he said, always checks the borrower first, just as a sensible shopkeeper checks a new customer.

A savings account, Mr Okafor said, is the simplest asset of all, and Leila already knew it better than any of the others. It pays a little interest, the bank holds her money until she asks for it, and in most places the amount is not expected to fall. For emergency money it is exactly the right tool, he said, so long as she does not ask it to do more.

Many countries protect bank deposits up to a fixed limit, so that savers do not lose everything if a bank fails, but the rules differ greatly from place to place. Mr Okafor urged her to find out exactly what protection applies where she lives, and to read the official page rather than a friend's opinion. It is the sort of dull homework, he said, that saves a person from very exciting problems.

Then Mr Okafor showed her a simple but important idea, which is that risk and reward usually travel together. Safe things tend to grow slowly and calmly, while riskier things may grow faster over many years, but they may also fall, and sometimes they fall hard. Nobody offers high reward without risk, he said, and anyone who claims to is selling something.

Mr Okafor lined up three glass jars on the shelf and labelled them in pencil: safe, steady and growing. The first was for cash and emergencies, the second for money needed in a few years, and the third for money that could wait for a very long time. A sensible person, he said, uses all three of the jars for different jobs, and never asks one jar to do the work of another.

That evening Leila drew three jars of her own in her notebook and wrote a small number beside each one. Almost everything she owned was in the first jar, and the other two were nearly empty, which she found oddly encouraging, because it meant that all of the choices still lay ahead. She wrote the date at the top of the page, so that one day she could look back and see how far the jars had come.

By now Leila had learned that assets come in many different kinds, from cash to bonds, from shares to rental homes, and from small businesses to tools. Each one has its own risk, its own reward and its own timing, and no single one is best for everybody. She was beginning to see the world as a long shelf with many different jars.

Leila put down her pencil and realised, rather suddenly, that none of this was magic, and that none of it required her to be clever. It was only a set of careful choices, made over many months, by someone who kept looking honestly at the numbers. That thought made the whole subject feel smaller and friendlier, like a garden she could finally walk into.

One early morning, before her shift at the garden centre, Leila walked past a small bakery whose lights were already blazing in the dark street. The smell of warm bread filled the cold air, and she stopped at the window to watch a man in a white apron lifting trays out of an enormous oven. She went inside, bought a warm roll for a dollar, and then began to ask the baker a great many questions.

The baker, Mr Haddad, laughed when she asked and said that a bakery has many more costs than people imagine, and flour was the smallest of them. He paid rent for the shop, wages for his two helpers, gas and electricity for the ovens, and a fee for the van, and the bread had to cover every one. Leila realised that she was looking at a business from the inside for the first time.

Mr Okafor, who bought his bread there every Saturday, told her later that a business is an asset only when its income beats its costs by a safe margin. The oven, the shop and the van are tools, and the profit is the proof that the tools are working. A business that loses money every month, he added, is a leaking bucket with a sign above the door.

Mr Haddad told her, with considerable pride, that two years earlier he had borrowed money to buy a larger oven. It allowed him to bake nearly twice as much bread in the early morning, when the demand was highest, and the extra sales covered the loan payments with some money left over. It was an example of good borrowing, Mr Okafor said, because the debt had bought something that earns.

Mr Haddad added, with a shrug, that not every week is a good one, and that the oven does not know the difference between a busy morning and an empty one. When it rains for days, fewer people come to the shop, and the bread that he cannot sell must be given away or thrown out. A business, he said with a smile, is an asset with moods, and the owner must learn to live with all of them.

Mr Okafor told Leila about a mistake from his own early years, and he seemed to enjoy telling it against himself. He had once spent a large part of his savings on a bright new sign for the front of Okafor Hardware, convinced that it would pull crowds of customers off the street. A few more people looked up at it, he said, but hardly any of them came in.

Soon afterwards he bought a second fridge for cold drinks, because so many hot and thirsty customers had asked for them during the summer. It cost far less than the sign had done, and it paid for itself within a single season, then went on earning for years. “One of those was decoration,” he said, “and the other was a small machine for making money.”

Mr Okafor explained that he had not simply guessed about the fridge, as he had guessed about the sign. For a whole month he kept a notepad beside the till and made a tally mark whenever a customer asked for a cold drink, and the marks soon made the decision for him. The numbers, he said, are almost always more honest than the hopes of the owner.

The lesson, Mr Okafor said, was to test small before spending big, whether the purchase is a fridge, a course or an investment. A small trial costs little and teaches a great deal, while a large mistake teaches exactly the same lesson for a much higher price. He wrote that sentence in Leila's notebook in his tidy capital letters, and underlined the word small, as he always did.

The next morning, Leila looked at the garden centre with entirely new eyes, and she was surprised how much she had never noticed before. The plants were stock that had to be sold before they wilted, the greenhouse was a costly tool, and the till was the place where the proof of everything finally arrived. She started to notice which plants sold best, and which ones sat on the shelf and quietly cost money.

Inspired by the bakery and by Mr Okafor's tidy notebooks, Leila signed up for an evening class in bookkeeping. It met twice a week in a plain classroom above the public library, and the fee was a few hundred dollars, which she paid from her savings after thinking about it for several days. It was the first time she had ever spent money on herself with a reason.

The tutor, Mrs Lind, was strict, tidy and secretly very funny, and she taught the class to write down every sale and every cost in the right column on the right day. She insisted that bookkeeping was not about arithmetic but about honesty, because a record that is kept truthfully will tell the truth in return. Leila recognised the idea at once, since it sounded exactly like something that Mr Okafor would say over a cup of ginger tea.

A skill, Mr Okafor told her, can be an asset in its own right, because it may raise the money that a person earns for the rest of her working life. It cannot be stolen, it will not lose its value in a market crash, and it usually grows more valuable the more that it is used. Leila had never thought of her own head as a place to keep assets.

Mr Okafor reminded her, though, that a course has a cost, and its benefit is never guaranteed, however attractive the leaflet may be. She had to weigh what it cost in money and evenings against what it might bring, and ask honestly whether the skill would be used. Not every course is an investment, he said, and some are simply an expensive hobby.

In class she practised with an imaginary shop that sold umbrellas, and she wrote down each sale and each cost in two neat columns. Every week she hunted down her own mistakes, and every week she found fewer of them, until the totals began to agree with each other. She discovered, to her own considerable surprise, that she enjoyed it a great deal more than she had ever expected to.

At the garden centre, Leila began to keep a neat sheet that showed which plants sold quickly and which ones sat on the benches for weeks. Her manager, Ms Rowan, noticed it pinned beside the greenhouse door one morning and asked, in a tone that gave nothing away, who had been so organised. Leila felt her face grow hot, and then she admitted that it was her.

Ms Rowan, who had been struggling to keep up with the paperwork, asked Leila to help with the shop's records for two hours each week and offered a small extra payment. It was not a fortune, but it was the first money Leila had ever earned with a skill that she had chosen to build. She accepted at once, and then walked home with an odd bounce in her step.

Mr Okafor added that health is another asset, though it will never appear in any list at the bank, and he spoke about it with a sudden gentleness. Sleep, decent food and a little exercise keep a person able to work and to think clearly, while neglect has costs that arrive later and are rarely small. He said that this was general common sense, not medical advice, and that she should ask a doctor about anything personal.

Time, Mr Okafor said, is the one thing that every person receives in exactly the same amount each day, and nobody can borrow more of it. How a person spends those twenty-four hours is part of how that person builds, or fails to build, everything else in her life. Leila looked at the hours she spent scrolling on her phone, and she did not enjoy the sight.

Dani, inspired by Leila's course, decided to follow her example and began to learn programming with a set of free online lessons during her lunch breaks. Mr Okafor smiled when he heard about it, and then he warned both of them that the best investment in skill is the one that a person actually finishes. A thousand half-opened courses, he said, are worth less than one good one that is completed.

Mr Okafor drew three arrows pointing at a single pocket, and he labelled them wages, business and assets. Every dollar that any person receives, he said, arrives through one of these three doors, and it is worth knowing which door is being used. Leila had thought about money so vaguely that she had never asked the question.

Wages are the first door, and it is the one that Leila used every day, trading hours of her life for dollars at a fixed rate. It is honest and dependable, and most people begin here, but when the working stops, the money stops with it. Mr Okafor said that there was no shame in this door, only a limit.

A business is the second door, and it earns money from the goods or services that it sells rather than from hours alone. A good business can eventually earn more than the owner could ever earn working by herself, but it asks for effort, risk and a great deal of patience. The bakery on the corner, Leila realised, was exactly this kind of door, and its owner had opened it with an oven and a loan.

The third door is the ownership of assets, which can pay a person even while she is asleep or on holiday. A rented flat sends rent, a savings account sends interest and a company's share may send a dividend, and none of them needs an alarm clock. Mr Okafor said that this door opens slowly, and that it usually has to be built from the first one.

Most people begin with wages, Mr Okafor assured her, and there is absolutely nothing wrong with beginning there. The wise step is to use a part of the wages to build the other doors, little by little, in the same way that a gardener plants a seed from the first harvest. She felt relieved, because she had feared that he might look down on a simple paycheque.

A few weeks later, Dani received a pay rise at the garden centre, and she celebrated by spending the whole of the extra amount on a larger flat, new shoes and more evenings out. Within two months she was exactly as short of money as she had been before, only now with a better address. It was a perfect, and slightly painful, lesson about how easily spending grows to fill an income.

Back in her notebook, Leila circled the small number at the very bottom of her monthly sums, the figure that remained once all her spending was taken from her income. For most of the past year it had been close to zero, and some months it had been below it. Seeing it circled in pencil made it look like a small, patient animal waiting to be fed.

Mr Okafor called this number the gap, and he declared it the most consequential figure in her whole notebook. It is the money left over after all the spending, and it is the only part of her pay that can ever become an asset, an emergency fund or a smaller debt. Everything else, he said, has already gone out of the door before the month is properly under way.

There are only two ways to make the gap larger, Mr Okafor said, and he drew one lever for each of them. A person can earn more, which takes time and skill, or spend less, which can start this very afternoon, and the best plans often pull both levers a little. Leila saw very clearly that the second lever was the one that was truly within her reach this afternoon.

Leila did a quick sum on the back of her hand with the pencil. If she could close even half of her four hundred dollars of leaks, her monthly gap would grow by about two hundred dollars, which was two thousand four hundred in a year. Suddenly the money that had seemed to vanish looked like something she might be able to catch.

On the next payday, Leila did something she had never done before: she moved some of her money into a jar marked future before she paid a single bill or bought a single thing. It felt strange, almost like cheating, as if the money had been hidden in a drawer where her own habits could not find it. She stood in the kitchen for a long moment, simply looking at the jar and wondering what her future self would say.

Mr Okafor called this habit paying yourself first, and he said that it was the simplest and most powerful trick in the whole subject. Most people save whatever happens to remain at the end of the month, he explained, and since spending expands to fill whatever room it is given, usually nothing remains at all. The wise way, he said, is to turn the whole order upside down, and to save first and spend whatever happens to be left.

To make it easier, Leila asked her bank to move the money automatically on every payday, so that she never had to decide again. Decisions, Mr Okafor said, are where most good intentions fail, and a system that works without willpower is worth far more than a hundred promises. After the first transfer had gone through, she found to her relief that she hardly noticed the money was missing from her account.

After some thought, Leila decided to save a fixed amount of two hundred and fifty dollars each month, which was a little more than half of what she hoped to save from her leaks. Mr Okafor approved, because he said it is far better to choose a modest amount that can be kept than a heroic one that will be abandoned by March. Consistency, he told her with a nod, is the quiet engine of this whole business, and it does not need to be exciting.

Before she bought any other kind of asset, Mr Okafor said, Leila needed an emergency fund, a store of cash for the day when something unexpected goes wrong. Without such a cushion, a lost job or a broken boiler can push a person into expensive debt within a single week. The fund is like a small umbrella, he said, and it is always cheaper to carry one than to be rained on.

Many financial educators suggest an emergency fund equal to three to six months of basic expenses, although the right figure depends on how secure a person's job is and who depends on her. For Leila, whose monthly basics came to a little over twelve hundred dollars, this was a target for the coming year rather than the coming month. She wrote the number on the inside cover of her notebook, where she would see it every time she opened the book.

One rainy morning on the way to work, Leila dropped her phone on the pavement, and the screen split across the middle like frozen water. A few weeks earlier she would have put the repair on a card and worried about it for months, but now she paid for it in cash from her small emergency fund. It was strangely satisfying, like watching an umbrella do exactly the job for which it had been bought on a rainy morning.

Dani laughed when she heard about the jar, the monthly transfers and the notebook, and said that Leila sounded as strict as a headmistress. A week later, after her own credit card bill had arrived, she quietly asked Leila to show her exactly how it was done. Leila realised, as she showed her friend the page, that she had never been prouder of anything she had ever learned.

Mr Okafor was careful to say that a money plan is not a diet, and that it should leave room for small, deliberate pleasures. A plan that allows no joy at all is quickly abandoned, he said, the way that harsh diets are, and then the old habits return with interest. Leila budgeted forty dollars a month for treats and was relieved to find that she could enjoy them without guilt.

At the end of the first month, Leila opened her banking app and found more money in her savings than she had ever managed to hold at once. It was not a fortune, and nobody would have been impressed by it, but it was proof that the plan worked and that the leaks could be stopped. She took a photograph of the number on her screen and carried it down the stairs to show Mr Okafor in person.

Mr Okafor placed a small balance scale on the table and put a pile of buttons on one side for the assets and a pile of pebbles on the other for the debts. The difference between the two, he said, is a person's net worth, and it is the single number that tells you which way you are moving. Leila stared at the little scale on the table, suddenly nervous about which side would turn out to be the heavier.

Leila wrote her assets in a neat column, and she tried hard to give each one an honest price rather than the one she had paid. Her savings, her laptop and her bicycle together came to a little over one thousand dollars, and she did not include the jacket, because nobody would buy it back at anything like the price. Mr Okafor nodded approvingly at that decision, and she noticed that he was trying very hard not to smile.

In the second column she wrote down her debts, the student loan and what remained on the phone plan, using the figures from the most recent statements. Together they came to more than three thousand dollars, which was already clearly larger than the first column, and she felt her stomach tighten. She forced herself to finish the sum anyway, because she knew that stopping halfway would only leave the fear in place.

Leila subtracted the debts from the assets, and the answer came out negative, about minus two thousand dollars. She owed roughly two thousand dollars more than she owned, and it was the first time she had ever seen that fact written down in her own handwriting. The pencil felt unexpectedly heavy in her fingers, and she put it down and watched the number for a long minute.

Leila's heart sank, and for a moment she wished that she had never started the exercise at all. She had imagined herself as an ordinary young woman with a small cushion of savings, and the page was telling her, quite politely, that this was not the whole truth. Her cheeks burned with embarrassment, even though nobody else was in the room to see the number on the page.

Mr Okafor rested one warm hand on the page and said gently that a negative net worth is extremely common for young people who have only just started to work. Many of them have borrowed to study and have had little time to build anything, so the number is not a verdict on their character, only on their age. “Nobody starts at the top of the hill,” he added, “and most of the people at the top once stood exactly where you are standing.”

Mr Okafor confided that when he first opened Okafor Hardware, he owed far more than he owned, and that his net worth had been much lower than hers, on paper. It took him almost six years of careful work, small savings and a stubborn refusal to buy things he did not need before the number crossed to the right side of zero. He said it without any drama or self-pity, in exactly the same tone that he might have used to describe the weather.

The number itself matters much less than its direction, Mr Okafor said, and he drew a small arrow in the margin that pointed upwards. If net worth rises over the months, the plan is working, and if it falls, something needs to change, and the sooner a person looks, the easier the change is. He suggested that she measure it once every three months and not every day, since a pot that is watched constantly seems never to boil.

Mr Okafor warned her to value each item at the price she could actually sell it for today, not at the price she had paid when it was new. A used laptop is rarely worth what it cost, and counting it at the old price only makes the net worth look better than it is. Honest figures, he said firmly, are the whole point of the exercise, and a flattering number is worse than no number at all.

Leila wrote her net worth and today's date on the first page of her notebook, in large, clear numbers that she could not pretend to misread. She was not happy about it, but she was strangely calm, as if she had finally put a heavy bag down on the floor and found that it did not move. The next page was blank and white, and she found, to her great surprise, that she could hardly wait to begin filling it.

Mr Okafor drew a ladder on the page, with a heavy weight hanging from its lowest rung, and he said that the first step is always to pay off the debt that costs the most. That means the one with the highest interest rate, because every dollar spent there removes the largest amount of future cost. Leila pulled her notebook closer and looked at her own two debts again, wondering which of them was the heavier.

Leila laid her two debts side by side on the table and circled the interest rate on each. The phone plan cost her about twelve percent a year, while the student loan cost only about four, so the smaller debt was the more expensive one, which surprised her. Size and cost, she realised with a small shock, were two completely different things, and she had been watching only the first.

Each month, Leila earned about one hundred dollars from her extra work on the garden centre's records, and she decided to send every dollar of it to the phone plan on top of the usual payment. It was money that she had never counted on, so she would not miss it, and it would be working at twelve percent against her debt. Mr Okafor smiled and said that this was the kind of sum he liked.

Mr Okafor reminded her to keep paying the required minimum on every single debt, so that none of them ever becomes late and attracts a penalty. All of the extra money, he said, should be pointed at one debt at a time, and the costliest is the one that deserves it first. Missing a payment, he added, costs more than almost any mistake with an investment.

Mr Okafor said honestly that some people prefer to pay off their smallest debt first, because a quick victory gives them the courage to carry on. It may cost a little more in interest than the other approach, but the feeling of progress can be worth a great deal to someone who is easily discouraged. He did not think that either way was shameful, and he told her that people differ in what keeps them going.

Both methods work, Mr Okafor said, and the best one is whichever a person is actually going to keep doing month after month. A perfect plan that is dropped by March is worth far less than a decent plan that is still running faithfully in December. Leila decided to go with the costliest debt first, because the arithmetic seemed to make her happy.

Month after month, Leila made her usual payment and added the extra hundred dollars from the garden centre records, and the balance fell steadily in her notebook. Five months later the phone plan was almost completely paid off, and each month there was a little less interest to charge. She had never before watched a number go down with such quiet pleasure, and she checked it every Sunday evening.

When Leila made the very last payment on the phone plan, she felt lighter than she had felt for a whole year, almost as if she had put down a suitcase. She celebrated in a way that suited her new habits, with a small cake from Mr Haddad's bakery, which she shared with Mr Okafor over tea. He said that a good celebration should cost less than the problem it marks.

The following month, the money that used to go to the phone plan was suddenly free, and Mr Okafor warned her that this is exactly the moment when habits quietly slip. Leila sent it on, together with the extra hundred dollars, to the student loan and to her emergency fund, so that it never had the chance to drift back into spending. A payment that already exists, he said, is far easier to redirect than a new one is to create from nothing.

Mr Okafor reminded her that student loans work very differently from country to country, and that nothing he said about them applied to every case. Some can be repaid early at no cost, some charge a fee for it, and some adjust with a person's income, so she should read her own terms and ask her lender if anything was unclear. If she ever fell behind, he added, the right step was to talk to the lender early, before the problem grew.

On a Saturday afternoon, Leila stopped outside a clothes shop with her short shopping list folded in her hand. A beautiful dark green coat in the window had caught her eye, and she could feel her old habit begin to stir, with its warm, persuasive voice. For a second she was almost certain that she would walk through the door.

She took a breath and asked herself the first question in her notebook, which was whether the coat was a need or only a want. She already owned a perfectly warm one, so the honest answer was that it was a want, and nothing about that was wrong, but it changed what the question really was. A want was allowed, she reminded herself, but it must be chosen on purpose.

On the back of her hand, in smudged pencil, were the three questions that Mr Okafor had taught her to ask before every purchase. Does it earn money, will it keep its value, and if the answer to both is no, is it a cost that she is truly happy to accept? The coat earned nothing, would be worth little next year, and was therefore a cost.

Mr Okafor's other rule, which she now remembered, was to wait thirty days before buying any want that is not cheap. Leila wrote the date in her phone, set a small reminder, and walked away from the window with a feeling that was more triumph than loss. By the time the reminder rang a month later, she hardly remembered the coat at all.

A few days later, her friends planned a birthday dinner at a very expensive restaurant, and Leila felt the familiar pressure to say yes and worry afterwards. Instead she took a deep breath and suggested a cheaper place that she knew, followed by a home-made dessert at her flat. To her relief, nobody complained, and two of her friends told her afterwards that they had been secretly worried about the bill.

Mr Okafor told her about a customer from his shop who had driven a very expensive car and worn beautiful suits. The man looked wealthy, but his loan payments were so large that one day he could not afford a ladder, and he had to ask to pay in small amounts. “What you see on the outside,” Mr Okafor said, “tells you what a person spends, and never what he owns.”

Some of the best savers that he had known, Mr Okafor added, drove old trucks, lived in small houses and wore the same coat for ten winters. They spent carefully, ignored every passing fashion and quietly owned a great deal more than their neighbours suspected. Leila thought of the shiny blue car in the garden centre car park and smiled to herself.

Mr Okafor stressed that money is meant to be spent, and that the goal is to spend it on the things that you truly value and to cut it from those that you do not. A person who loves music or books, he said, need not feel the slightest guilt about buying them, so long as the gap is protected first. Leila sat quietly for a while and thought about which of her old habits she had never really enjoyed at all.

The price on the tag, Mr Okafor reminded her, is only the first chapter of a longer story, because owning almost anything has running costs. A large television needs a stand, power and perhaps a repair, and a puppy needs food, training and visits to the vet for many years. She decided that she would always ask what a thing would cost her after the day of buying it.

In the end, Leila bought something that she had really needed, a sturdy pair of work boots that were on sale at the end of the season. She would wear them every day at the garden centre for years, and when she divided the price by the number of days, each wear cost her only a few cents. It was not an asset in the strict sense, but it was a wise cost.

In his drawing, Mr Okafor held a large shield over a house, a car and a savings jar, and he wrote the word insurance beneath it. Insurance, he explained, is a regular cost that protects a person's assets from losses so large that they could never pay for them alone. It does not put money in your pocket every month, but it may save you from losing the whole pocket.

Many people pay a small amount to the insurance company, and the company uses the pool of money to pay for the large losses of the few who suffer them. Mr Okafor remembered a fire in a neighbouring shop that would have ended the owner's business, if he had not been insured, and he said that he had renewed his own policy that same afternoon. It is a cost, he said, but it is a sensible one, in the same way that a good lock on a door is sensible.

She should insure the things whose loss would truly harm her, Mr Okafor advised, and not every small possession that a salesperson happens to mention. A broken toaster is a nuisance that most people can afford, but a flooded home, a car accident or a long illness can wreck a whole life. He reminded her that the right cover depends on her country, and that she should compare policies carefully.

Leila sat down with the small print of the insurance that came with her rented room, and she read it carefully, line by line. She discovered that her laptop was covered only up to a small amount and her bicycle not at all, and she decided that the bicycle, at least, deserved a better lock. Reading the policy, she found, was a good deal more interesting than she had feared.

Tax, Mr Okafor said, is another cost that every serious saver has to understand, and it is the one most likely to cause confusion. The rules differ from country to country and change from year to year, so anything he told her could only be a rough outline, and she should check the official rules for her own home. He had no wish, he added with a chuckle, to turn her into an accountant by accident or to give her the wrong answer.

In many places, money earned from interest, rent or the sale of shares may be taxed, and some special savings accounts are treated differently by the law. Mr Okafor said that these details can noticeably change how much she keeps in the end, which is why it is worth learning what is allowed in her own country. He did not name any rule, since he did not wish to be wrong.

Neat records, Mr Okafor assured her, make tax much easier and decisions much clearer, and her bookkeeping course had already given her half of the skill. A shoebox full of crumpled receipts, he said, is a miserable way to meet the end of the year, and it is surprisingly easy to avoid. She promised to keep her receipts in a folder and to label it clearly.

No asset is truly certain, Mr Okafor told her, not even the ones that feel the safest, because prices, banks, jobs and even countries can change. A safety net does not stop a fall from happening, but it makes the fall much smaller, and most of his advice, he said, was simply different ways of weaving the net. Leila thought of the emergency fund and the three jars on his shelf, and she began to see them as one connected net.

He told her to keep some money safe, some steady and some growing, and to match each jar to the time at which she would need it. The nearer the need, the safer the jar should be, and the more distant the need, the more patient she can afford to be with it. Leila added a small note to her notebook, with arrows pointing from each jar to a date.

Mr Okafor ended the lesson with a serious warning about anyone who promises quick riches with no risk at all, whether on the phone, on the internet or in a friendly conversation. If an offer sounds too good to be true, he said, it nearly always is, and the proper response is to stop, ask for everything in writing and, if in doubt, walk away. He had seen good, sensible people lose a lifetime of savings to very charming voices, and it had left him angry for years.

Time, Mr Okafor said, is the quiet partner of anyone who owns assets, and it works hardest for those who start early and stay calm. A tree does not grow in a week, and a pile of savings does not turn into security in a month, but a small amount added regularly for many years can become something remarkable. The people who struggle most, he had noticed, are often the ones who expect results too soon.

Mr Okafor led her out to his small back yard and showed her a lemon tree so heavy with fruit that its branches had to be propped up with sticks. He had planted it as a thin green stick when his daughter was born, nearly thirty years earlier, and for the first three years it had produced nothing at all. “Almost everything good,” he said, “is boring for a very long time before it is anything else, and then one day it bears fruit.”

After the phone plan was paid and her emergency fund had begun to look healthy, Leila thought about the third jar, the one marked growing. After weeks of careful reading, she decided to put a very small amount into a broad fund with low fees, and Mr Okafor reminded her that this was her own choice and not his advice. She wrote down all of her reasons in the notebook, in plain words, before she clicked on anything at all.

In the autumn, Mr Okafor travelled to visit his daughter in a faraway city for a month, and before he left he gave Leila his old watering can and a firm instruction to keep her plan. For the first time since that first Sunday, she was entirely on her own, and she was surprised by how quiet the stairs seemed. She watered his ginger plants every morning, out of a mixture of duty and loneliness.

One grey week in October, the news announced that share prices had fallen sharply, and the television presenter's voice was heavy with concern. When Leila opened her account, the value of her small fund had dropped by several percent, and her first instinct was to sell everything and make the discomfort stop. Her hand was actually on the screen when she remembered the man in Mr Okafor's story.

She put the phone face down on the table and opened her notebook to the page about the three jars, and read it slowly. This money was in the growing jar, which meant that it was meant for many years from now, and a fall this week did not change the date on which she would need it. She closed the notebook, made a cup of ginger tea and left the account alone.

At lunch the next day, Dani asked whether Leila was worried about the fall in prices, and what she would do if she were in Dani's position. Leila found herself repeating, almost word for word, the questions that Mr Okafor had taught her, and she was careful to say that she was not an expert and that her own situation was not Dani's. They agreed, in the end, to look at the facts together over the weekend and to decide nothing in a panic.

A month later, prices had recovered a little, though not completely, and Leila's small fund was worth slightly more than the first time she had looked. She kept saving her fixed amount every payday, whatever the news said, and she was careful not to treat the recovery as a victory or the fall as a disaster. It was only one small bend in a very long road, and she meant to keep walking along it for many years.

Mr Okafor came back from his trip with a battered suitcase and a small gift of tea from his daughter's city, and he found Leila waiting on the stairs with her notebook. He turned every page slowly while she watched his face, and for a long time he said nothing at all, which made her more nervous than any lecture. Then he looked up at her, and she saw to her astonishment that his eyes were bright with something that looked very like pride.

Over tea, Leila wrote her plan on a fresh page in four short lines, so that it would be easy to remember on a bad day. Save a fixed amount first, track every dollar of spending, pay the costliest debt before the cheaper ones, and test small before spending big. Mr Okafor read it twice, and then he asked her to sign and date the page, as he did with his own accounts.

A year after that first Sunday, Leila sat at her kitchen table with a thick notebook that was almost full of her own handwriting. She turned back to the very first page, where her net worth stood in large, honest numbers, and she looked at it for a long moment without flinching. It was exactly where she had left it, and it was not where she was.

On a fresh page, she listed everything that she now owned and everything that she still owed, valuing each item honestly. The phone plan had vanished from the debts, the student loan was noticeably smaller, and her savings, emergency fund and small fund all showed larger numbers than before. She did the sum twice, slowly and carefully, because she wanted to be perfectly sure before she allowed herself to feel anything.

When she subtracted, the new number was almost four thousand dollars higher than the one on the first page, and for the first time it stood above zero. She let out a long, shaky breath and laughed, partly from relief and partly because she was a little disbelieving. Nobody had given her a penny of it, and no stroke of luck had arrived to help.

Leila could see exactly where the change had come from, and it was almost embarrassingly ordinary. The leaks had been plugged, the saving had happened automatically on every payday, the costly phone plan had been paid off first, and a small new skill had brought in some extra income. Nothing in the whole list was clever or secret, and everything in it was simply repeated, month after month, until it worked.

Over tea that Sunday, Mr Okafor asked Leila what she thought she had really learned during the year, and he leaned back to listen. She said that money was not about being clever, as she had once feared, but mostly about looking honestly at the numbers and then acting on what she saw. He nodded slowly, as though she had just read aloud a page from his own notebook.

Dani burst through the door one evening, waving her latest credit card statement, and the balance on it was much smaller than it had been a year earlier. She had stopped using the card for small purchases, she paid far more than the minimum every month, and she had even begun to save something on the side. Leila hugged her friend warmly, and then they both looked a little embarrassed and quickly went to put the kettle on.

Leila's younger brother, Tomas, who was fifteen and always short of pocket money, came to visit for the weekend. She took a sheet of paper, wrote the one question across the top in large pencil letters, and watched his face with a feeling that she could not quite name. It was the question that Mr Okafor had once written for her, and now it was being passed on.

Tomas tried the question first on his games console, and he saw at once that it took money out of his pocket and put none back in. Then he tried it on his new trainers, and he admitted, with a sheepish grin, that he was not sure which column they belonged in. Leila laughed, because that was almost exactly what had happened to her a year before.

Mr Okafor, who had been standing quietly in the doorway with a teapot in his hands, stepped forward and smiled at both of them. He told Leila that the pencil and the notebook were now truly hers, and that the lesson was hers to pass on, as it had once been passed to him. Then he sat down with them, and he poured three cups of ginger tea.

On that bright Sunday afternoon, Mr Okafor reminded them that everything he had shared was a set of general principles, not personal advice for any one person or country. If you remember only one thing, he said, ask what a thing does for your money, put the answer on paper, and then act on it. Leila smiled, sipped her ginger tea, and turned to a fresh page of the notebook, ready for whatever the next year would hold.
